question: A 22-year-old female presents at 24 weeks gestation with a chief complaint of burning upon urination. On physical exam, you note a gravid uterus that extends above the umbilicus. A urine analysis and culture is sent demonstrating over 100,000 colony forming units of E. coli. Of note this patient had a similar UTI 7 weeks ago that was resolved with appropriate medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?

options.opd: Nitrofurantoin and continue with nitrofurantoin prophylaxis for the rest of the pregnancy
options.ope: Cephalexin and IV antibiotic prophylaxis for the rest of the pregnancy

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: UTI caused by E. coli -> previous UTI 7 weeks ago -> resolved with appropriate medication -> 80% CHAIN: UTI in pregnancy -> increased risk of complications -> prompt treatment necessary -> 85% CHAIN: Nitrofurantoin -> commonly used for uncomplicated UTIs -> safe in pregnancy -> 90% CHAIN: Nitrofurantoin appropriate for UTI in pregnancy -> effective against E. coli -> 85% CHAIN: Nitrofurantoin and continue with nitrofurantoin prophylaxis for the rest of the pregnancy -> recommended management for recurrent UTIs in pregnancy -> 80%
enhanced_information: Nitrofurantoin is a commonly used and safe antibiotic for uncomplicated UTIs, including in pregnancy. It is effective against E. coli, the causative agent in this case. Therefore, the most appropriate management for this patient would be Nitrofurantoin.
analysis: The core medical principle for managing UTIs in pregnancy is to use antibiotics that are safe for both the mother and the fetus. Nitrofurantoin is considered safe and effective for treating uncomplicated UTIs in pregnancy, including those caused by E. coli. It is the preferred choice for this patient based on consensus guidelines.
